# Plugin Registries and Extensibility {#sec-plugins}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

The vision statement in Chapter 1 listed extensibility as one of
NebulaStream's three pillars. This chapter is about how that pillar
is built — specifically, how a plugin (a new source, sink,
formatter, operator, or rewrite rule) gets compiled into the engine
and made discoverable at runtime, all while staying compatible with
C++'s static linking model.

The mechanism is a *static plugin registry*, generated by CMake at
build time. It is one of the more interesting pieces of build-system
engineering in NebulaStream and well worth understanding before you
add your first plugin.

---

## 13.1 The problem static plugins solve {#sec-static-plugin-problem}

Plugins exist to keep the engine modular. A core team can ship the
engine; third parties can ship sources, sinks, and rewrite rules
without touching the core code. The engine discovers plugins at
runtime via a registry; user code in the engine looks up "TCP"
in the source registry and gets back a factory function for
constructing TCP sources.

The implementation challenge is that C++ is a static-linking
language. Unlike Java or Python, where adding a class to the
classpath at runtime is a normal thing, C++ wants every symbol
resolved at link time. There are dynamic loading mechanisms
(`dlopen`, `LoadLibrary`) but they are awkward for production
deployments and disastrous for embedded targets.

NebulaStream's solution: every plugin is statically linked, *and*
self-registers into a global registry at startup. This is the
classic "register a class with itself" pattern. The trick is doing
it without falling into the **Static Initialisation Order Fiasco**
(SIOF) — the well-known C++ pitfall where the order of static
initialisations across translation units is undefined.

The full solution is documented in
`docs/design/20240701_static_plugin_registry.md`. The mechanism has
five stated goals (G1–G5):

- **G1**: Plugins must be statically linkable and self-register.
- **G2**: Internal vs. external plugins must be cleanly separated.
- **G3**: The mechanism must work for many extension types
  (sources, sinks, operators, types, functions, rewrite rules).
- **G4**: Registration must be guaranteed (no "I forgot to declare
  this static instance" failures).
- **G5**: Must not depend on initialisation order.

The fix for G5 is what makes the design interesting.

---

## 13.2 The CMake macros {#sec-cmake-macros}

A plugin author writes their plugin and one CMake macro
invocation. The macros live in
`/Users/zeuchste/git/nebulastream/cmake/PluginRegistrationUtil.cmake`.
The two main entry points:

```cmake
# nes-plugins/CMakeLists.txt
activate_optional_plugin("Sources/TCPSource" ON)
activate_optional_plugin("Sources/GeneratorSource" ON)
activate_optional_plugin("Sinks/VoidSink" ON)
activate_optional_plugin("InputFormatters/JSONInputFormatter" ON)
activate_optional_plugin("OutputFormatters/JSONOutputFormatter" ON)
if (NES_ENABLES_TESTS)
    activate_optional_plugin("Sinks/ChecksumSink" ON)
endif()
```

`activate_optional_plugin` turns on an optional plugin in the
build. There is a corresponding `add_plugin` for built-in plugins
that ship in the engine without an opt-in toggle.

What the macros actually do, behind the scenes, is generate a
`Registrar` class — a single C++ file that contains, for each
active plugin, the registration call. The generation is in
`generate_plugin_registrar`:

```cmake
# cmake/PluginRegistrationUtil.cmake (excerpt)
function(generate_plugin_registrar current_dir current_binary_dir
                                   plugin_registry plugin_registry_component)
    set(registrar_header_template_path
        ${current_dir}/registry/templates/${plugin_registry}GeneratedRegistrar.inc.in)
    file(READ ${registrar_header_template_path} registrar_header_file_data)

    foreach (reg_func IN LISTS plugin_registry_plugin_names_final)
        list(APPEND REGISTER_FUNCTION_DECLARATIONS
             "${plugin_registry}RegistryReturnType Register${reg_func}${plugin_registry}(${plugin_registry}RegistryArguments)")
        list(APPEND REGISTER_ALL_FUNCTION_CALLS
             "registry.addEntry(\"${reg_func}\", Register${reg_func}${plugin_registry})")
    endforeach ()

    configure_file(${temp_registrar_header_template_file}
                   ${registrar_header_generated_path} @ONLY)
endfunction()
```

The template file (`<Type>GeneratedRegistrar.inc.in`) declares
forward declarations for every plugin's `Register*` function and a
single `registerAll` method that calls each. The plugin author
provides the `Register*` function in their plugin code; CMake
generates the file that calls them all.

---

## 13.3 The eager-init escape from SIOF {#sec-siof-escape}

The Static Initialisation Order Fiasco arises when one global
constructor uses another that has not yet been constructed.
Self-registration through `static MyPlugin instance{}` traditionally
suffers from this: which plugin's constructor runs first? Which
finds the registry already initialised?

NebulaStream sidesteps this with **explicit initialisation**:

- The registry is *not* a global. It is created on-demand when
  first accessed (Meyers' singleton pattern), so its lifetime
  begins at first use.
- Plugin registration is *not* a static constructor. It is a
  function call inside `registerAll`, which is invoked explicitly
  from `main()` (or an equivalent fixed initialisation point in
  the worker startup).

The result is that registration order is well-defined: it is the
order of `registerAll`'s sequential calls. The compiler is not
asked to make any guarantee about cross-translation-unit
ordering.

This is, in retrospect, the obvious solution. Most "self-registering
plugin" patterns in C++ get this wrong; NebulaStream's design is one
of the cleaner implementations I have seen.

---

## 13.4 The plugin types {#sec-five-plugin-types}

NebulaStream's plugin system is generic. The currently-supported
extension types:

| Type | Registry | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Source | `SourceRegistry` | TCP, File, Generator, Network |
| Sink | `SinkRegistry` | File, Print, Void, Checksum, Network |
| InputFormatter | `InputFormatIndexerRegistry` | CSV, JSON, Native |
| OutputFormatter | `OutputFormatterRegistry` | CSV, JSON, Native |
| LoweringRule | `LoweringRuleRegistry` | HashJoin, NLJoin |
| LogicalFunction | `LogicalFunctionRegistry` | arithmetic, comparison, UDFs |

The "Network" sources and sinks moved from the optional-plugin
tier to the built-in tier alongside the distribution layer
(Chapter 19) — they are how operators on different workers
communicate.

Each registry has the same shape: a string-keyed map from a type
name to a factory function. The factory takes a descriptor (which
encodes type-specific configuration) and returns an instance.

An earlier draft of this chapter listed a future-direction
`FunctionRegistry`. That registry has since landed: see
`nes-logical-operators/registry/include/LogicalFunctionRegistry.hpp`,
which lets new logical functions be plugin-registered alongside
sources, sinks, and formatters. The `RewriteRuleRegistry` for
optimiser rules remains a future direction. The same CMake
template machinery supports both without further engineering;
the framework was designed for it.

---

## 13.5 Adding a new source: a worked example {#sec-add-source}

Adding a new source plugin is the canonical "hello world" of
NebulaStream extensibility. The full walkthrough is in
`docs/guide/extensibility.md` and `docs/guide/how_to_add_a_source.md`.
The shape:

1. Create a new directory under
   `nes-plugins/Sources/`*MySource*`/` (alongside the existing
   `nes-plugins/Sources/TCPSource/`) with a `CMakeLists.txt` and
   the plugin's source files.
2. The `CMakeLists.txt` calls `add_plugin_as_library` with the
   plugin name and the registry it belongs to.
3. The plugin's source provides a `Register*` function that the
   generated `Registrar` will call. The function body adds the
   factory function to the registry.
4. Activate the plugin in `nes-plugins/CMakeLists.txt` with
   `activate_optional_plugin("Sources/MySource" ON)`.
5. Rebuild. The CMake regeneration picks up the new entry, the
   `Registrar` is regenerated, the worker's startup code calls the
   plugin's `Register*`, and "MySource" is now a valid `TYPE` in
   `CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE` statements.

That is the entire user-facing surface: write a class, write a
register function, add a CMake line, rebuild. No symbol-table
contortions, no dynamic loading, no `dlopen`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: how Telegraf and PostgreSQL handle this"}
Telegraf's plugin system is a register-by-function-pointer
pattern in Go, which has language-level support for `init()`
functions that the runtime calls at startup. The mechanism is
much simpler than NebulaStream's CMake template machinery — but
of course it requires a runtime. C++ does not have one.

PostgreSQL's plugin system is dynamic: shared libraries
(`postgresql-contrib` packages) are loaded with `LOAD 'mymodule'`
at runtime, with each module's `_PG_init()` doing registration.
This is more flexible (you can add modules without rebuilding the
server) but more dangerous (ABI compatibility is the user's
problem) and not viable for embedded deployments.

NebulaStream's static-linked, CMake-generated registrar is the
right answer for an engine targeting edge deployments where
runtime dynamic loading is awkward and a rebuild is the
expected mode of customisation.
:::

---

## Summary {#sec-ch13-summary}

NebulaStream's plugin system is a static plugin registry generated
at CMake-time. The framework supports sources, sinks, input/output
formatters, and lowering rules through a single uniform mechanism:
a string-keyed factory registry, populated by an explicitly-called
`registerAll` function whose body is generated by CMake from a
template. The design avoids the Static Initialisation Order Fiasco
by replacing constructor-time self-registration with explicit
initialisation. Adding a new plugin is a directory, a CMake line,
and a `Register*` function — no dynamic loading, no manual
registry edits.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch13-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 13.1: examine the generated registrar"}
After a build, find the generated `Registrar` files in your
build directory:

```shell
find cmake-build-debug -name '*GeneratedRegistrar*'
```

Open one — say, the `SourceGeneratedRegistrar` — and read it.
Confirm that every active source plugin appears, and that the
function called from `registerAll` matches the plugin's
hand-written `Register*` function.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 13.2: deactivate a plugin"}
In `nes-plugins/CMakeLists.txt`, change one
`activate_optional_plugin(... ON)` to `OFF` for, say, the JSON
formatter. Rebuild. What happens when you try to use the JSON
formatter? You should get a binding error that the formatter
type is unknown — caught by the registry lookup at query
submission, not at runtime.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 13.3: a tiny new sink"}
Sketch a `BlackHoleSink` that discards every record. The sink
class is about 20 lines (`execute` does nothing). The
registration is one CMake line and one `Register*` function.
You do not need to actually build it; the exercise is to see
how minimal the boilerplate is.
:::
